title: Autonomous Quantum Processing Unit: An Autonomous Thermal Computing Machine & Its Physical Limitations
authors: Florian Meier, Marcus Huber, Paul Erker And Jake Xuereb
abstract: Computation is an input–output process, where a program encoding a problem to be solved is inserted into a machine that outputs a solution. Quantum computation conventionally relies on classical, external control outside the quantum computer to execute a program, obscuring computational and thermodynamic resources required. To understand the fundamental limits of computation, however, it is pivotal to work with a fully self-contained description of a quantum computation modeling the resources on the same footing as the computation itself. By developing a framework that we dub the autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) we model quantum computation in the framework of autonomous thermal machines. Consisting of an internal quantum timekeeping mechanism, instruction register and memory system the aQPU allows investigating relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed and fidelity of a desired quantum computation.
tldr: The paper introduces an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) as a thermal machine, modeling quantum computation with internal resources to study thermodynamic costs and limitations.
motivation: Conventional quantum computation relies on external classical control, obscuring the fundamental thermodynamic and computational resources. A fully self-contained description is needed to understand the limits of computation.
method: The authors develop a framework for an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) that includes an internal quantum clock, instruction register, and memory, treating computation as a thermal machine process.
result: The framework allows investigation of relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed, and fidelity of quantum computations, revealing trade-offs and fundamental limits.
conclusion: The aQPU provides a unified model to study the physical resources required for quantum computation, bridging quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Distributing Graph States With A Photon-weaving Quantum Server
authors: Daniel Bhatti And Kenneth Goodenough
abstract: One of the key aims of quantum networks is the efficient distribution of multipartite entangled states among end users. While various architectures have been proposed, each comes with distinct advantages and limitations. Many designs depend on long-lived quantum memories and deterministic gates, which, while powerful, introduce considerable cost and technical challenges. Experimentally cheaper alternatives that circumvent these constraints are often limited to specific types of entanglement and a specific number of users. Here, we present an experiment-friendly quantum server that relies only on linear optical elements, offering a flexible approach to multipartite entanglement distribution. Our so-called photon-weaving quantum server can generate and distribute one of several locally nonequivalent graph states, including Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states, as well as path, cycle, and caterpillar graph states. This is achieved through two distinct fusion protocols, i.e. multiphoton graph-state fusion (graph-state weaving) and multiphoton GHZ-state fusion (GHZ-state weaving), and can readily be implemented.
tldr: Proposes an experiment-friendly quantum server using linear optics to distribute various graph states among end users.
motivation: Efficient distribution of multipartite entangled states is key for quantum networks, but existing architectures often require costly long-lived quantum memories and deterministic gates.
method: The server uses two fusion protocols (graph-state weaving and GHZ-state weaving) with only linear optical elements to generate and distribute graph states like GHZ, path, cycle, and caterpillar states.
result: The photon-weaving server can generate several locally nonequivalent graph states, offering flexibility in entanglement distribution without the need for quantum memories or deterministic gates.
conclusion: This approach provides a practical, scalable solution for multipartite entanglement distribution in quantum networks, potentially lowering experimental barriers.

title: Phase-controlled Thermal Amplification In A Quantum Thermal Transistor
authors: Xiaoyun Wang And Dazhi Xu
abstract: We investigate phase-controlled heat transport in a quantum thermal transistor composed of three coupled two-level systems, each connected to an independent thermal reservoir. Using a nonsecular Redfield master equation, we show that a gauge-invariant phase in the triangular coupling loop provides an efficient control knob beyond reservoir temperatures: at fixed temperature bias, tuning the phase strongly modulates the steady-state heat currents and can generate pronounced thermal amplification, whereby a small variation of the control current induces large changes in the currents at the other two terminals. We further analyze how the amplification depends on the reservoir temperature as well as on the intersystem couplings, identifying regimes of enhanced performance. To clarify the underlying mechanism, we develop a complementary weak-coupling theory based on a local Lindblad equation and second-order cumulant expansion. This analysis shows that the phase first enters the exchange coherences and is then transferred to the populations through loop interference, while the heat currents are dominated by the resulting population corrections. Our results establish phase engineering as a flexible route to regulating heat flow and thermal amplification in multi-terminal quantum thermal devices.
tldr: A quantum thermal transistor using three coupled two-level systems achieves phase-controlled heat amplification.
motivation: To demonstrate that a gauge-invariant phase in the coupling loop can modulate heat currents and provide thermal amplification beyond temperature control.
method: Uses a nonsecular Redfield master equation and a complementary local Lindblad approach with second-order cumulant expansion to analyze steady-state heat transport.
result: Tuning the phase strongly modulates heat currents and generates pronounced thermal amplification; phase enters exchange coherences and transfers to populations via loop interference.
conclusion: Phase engineering offers a flexible route to regulate heat flow and amplification in multi-terminal quantum thermal devices.

title: Heralded Ultrafast Generation Of Macroscopic Quantum States In Matter With Bright Squeezed Vacuum Light
authors: Shohei Imai
abstract: We show that bright squeezed vacuum light, combined with a single-shot quadrature measurement of the post-interaction light, enables the ultrafast generation of macroscopic quantum states in matter. Although in the weak-coupling regime multiphoton quantum light leaves the unconditional matter state as a classical mixture due to light–matter entanglement, quadrature-based heralding prepares the matter in a Gaussian-weighted quantum superposition of laser-driven matter states. For an ensemble of resonantly electric-dipole-coupled two-level systems, this heralding dynamics acts as a Gaussian filter with respect to the electric polarization, with brighter squeezed-vacuum light accelerating the preparation of the zero-eigenvalue Dicke state. Counter-rotating terms further drive a stroboscopic transition from this Dicke state to a cat-like state. Our results open a route to ultrafast engineering of macroscopic quantum matter with strong-field quantum light.
tldr: Bright squeezed vacuum light combined with quadrature measurement enables ultrafast generation of macroscopic quantum states in matter.
motivation: To achieve ultrafast preparation of macroscopic quantum states in matter using multiphoton quantum light, overcoming the limitation of weak coupling where unconditional states become classical mixtures.
method: The authors propose a heralding scheme based on single-shot quadrature measurement of bright squeezed vacuum light after interaction with an ensemble of two-level systems, which acts as a Gaussian filter on the matter state.
result: The heralding prepares the matter in a Gaussian-weighted superposition of laser-driven states, accelerating the preparation of the zero-eigenvalue Dicke state, and counter-rotating terms drive a transition to a cat-like state.
conclusion: This work opens a route to ultrafast engineering of macroscopic quantum matter using strong-field quantum light, relevant for hybrid quantum systems combining light and matter.

title: Non-Markovian Quantum Mpemba Effect In Strongly Correlated Quantum Dots
authors: Yuandong Wang And Jianhua Wei
abstract: Harnessing non-Markovian effects has emerged as a resource for quantum control, where a structured environment can act as a quantum memory. We investigate the quench dynamics from specific initial states to equilibrium steady states in strongly correlated quantum dot systems. The distance between quantum states is quantified using the Bures metric, which endows the space of reduced density matrices with a Riemannian geometric structure. Using the numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion method, we demonstrate a quantum Mpemba effect (QME) arising from non-Markovianity. Unlike previous studies centered on non-interacting limits, we reveal a distinct non-Markovian QME uniquely driven by the initial-state-dependent formation of the many-body Kondo resonance. Furthermore, by tracking the dynamical evolution in the generalized Bloch parameter space, we uncover an intrinsic QME. This trajectory-dependent analysis provides a rigorous geometric perspective on the circuitous relaxation pathways driven by Kondo correlations. Our results underscore the critical role of memory effects in quantum quench dynamics and suggest new pathways for controlling anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a non-Markovian quantum Mpemba effect in strongly correlated quantum dots, driven by Kondo correlations and memory effects.
motivation: Understanding anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems is important for quantum control; the quantum Mpemba effect offers a way to harness non-Markovianity.
method: The authors use the numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion method to simulate quench dynamics and quantify state distance via the Bures metric.
result: They reveal a distinct non-Markovian QME uniquely driven by initial-state-dependent formation of the many-body Kondo resonance, and uncover an intrinsic QME via geometric analysis in Bloch parameter space.
conclusion: Memory effects play a critical role in quantum quench dynamics, and the findings suggest new pathways for controlling anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems.

title: Saturation Attack Of The Microwave-propagated Continuous Variable Quantum Key Distribution In Open Air
authors: Wenqi Peng, Xuan Li, Yongxin Feng, Xiu-Bo Chen And Ying Guo
abstract: Continuous variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) can achieve the secure communication between two distant legitimate users. The microwave CVQKD exhibits stronger robustness than the optical CVQKD in transmitting quantum signals and accordingly has broad application prospects in quantum networks. Although the microwave CVQKD does not rely on the traditional optical fibers to transmit quantum signals, its practical security is still vulnerable to saturation attacks. In view of this security vulnerability, we generalize saturation attacks to microwave CVQKD and clarify the impact of saturation attacks on the parameter estimation of microwave systems. Two saturation attack schemes are further compared, one based on displacement control alone and the other on joint displacement and gain control. To mitigate the negative impacts caused by this attack, we propose a countermeasure based on the quantum nearest neighbor algorithm, which can detect saturation attacks by measuring unknown quantum states. In addition, the influence of microwave antennas on the security of the communication system is assessed, confirming that antenna gain plays a key role in determining both the secret key rate and the maximum transmission distance.
tldr: This paper generalizes saturation attacks to microwave CVQKD and proposes a countermeasure using quantum nearest neighbor algorithm.
motivation: Microwave CVQKD offers robust quantum signal transmission but is vulnerable to saturation attacks; the paper aims to analyze and mitigate this security threat.
method: The authors model two saturation attack schemes (displacement control alone vs. joint displacement and gain control) and propose a detection countermeasure based on quantum nearest neighbor algorithm.
result: The analysis shows that antenna gain significantly impacts secret key rate and maximum transmission distance; the proposed countermeasure can detect saturation attacks.
conclusion: Saturation attacks pose a practical security risk to microwave CVQKD, but can be mitigated with appropriate detection methods, highlighting the importance of antenna design.

title: Capturing An Electron In The Virtual State
authors: Alok Nath Singh, Bibek Bhandari, Rafael Sánchez And Andrew N Jordan
abstract: We address a foundational question in quantum mechanics: can a particle be directly found in a classically-forbidden virtual state? We instantiate this conceptual question by investigating the traversal of electrons through a tunnel barrier, which we define in a triple quantum dot system where the occupation of the central dot is energetically avoided. The motivation behind this setup is to answer whether the central dot is occupied or not during a virtual transition when it is being explicitly monitored. We investigate this problem in two different limits of continuous measurements: the stochastic quantum diffusion and the quantum jump. We find that, even though individual trajectories differ considerably across these limits, measuring leads to a higher occupation in the central dot on average. We also find that a suitably strong measurement can significantly boost the tunneling current—an effect we call measurement-assisted tunneling. Our results demonstrate that the act of observation fundamentally reshapes tunneling dynamics, resolving the seeming paradox of detecting a particle in a classically forbidden region: weak measurements partially localize the particle, while strong measurements enforce a discontinuous either/or detection or no detection outcome.
tldr: This paper investigates whether an electron can be detected in a classically forbidden virtual state by monitoring a triple quantum dot system, revealing measurement-assisted tunneling.
motivation: To resolve the paradox of detecting a particle in a virtual state and understand how continuous measurement reshapes tunneling dynamics.
method: The authors model a triple quantum dot with energetically avoided central dot occupation and analyze two continuous measurement limits: stochastic quantum diffusion and quantum jumps.
result: Measurements increase average occupation of the central dot, and strong measurement can boost tunneling current, an effect called measurement-assisted tunneling.
conclusion: The act of observation fundamentally alters tunneling, with weak measurements partially localizing the particle and strong measurements enforcing discontinuous detection outcomes.

title: Steady-state Entanglement Harvesting For Two Rotating Atoms In A Cylindrical Cavity
authors: Hong-Tao Zheng, Xiang-Fa Zhou, Guang-Can Guo And Zheng-Wei Zhou
abstract: We study the entanglement dynamics of two rotating atoms (with two internal levels and ) in a cylindrical cavity, which interact with a massless scalar field in vacuum satisfying the Dirichlet boundary condition. Our analysis demonstrates that it is possible to obtain the steady-state entanglement under two types of resonant conditions. For two identical atoms with the same world-line, the system reduces to the usual dissipative Dicke model at the first resonant condition where and are the energy splitting and the angular velocity of the th atom, and is the Lorentz factor. The entangled steady-state takes the form where and are constant, which is consistent with the previous study (see 2022 Phys. Rev. D 106 105028). For two atoms with different world-lines, the system suffers from a significant mixed joint dissipation process at the second resonant condition , and reaches an entangled steady-state as . Moreover, with the help of the cavity, we can obtain a much higher concurrence in the final states by changing the relative ratio of the two orbital radii. Our work thus provides a more effective way for the extraction of steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect for two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity.
tldr: This paper studies steady-state entanglement harvesting from vacuum for two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity, using the analogue Unruh effect.
motivation: To understand how motion and boundary conditions affect entanglement extraction from quantum vacuum, and to achieve steady-state entanglement for practical quantum information tasks.
method: The authors model two two-level atoms rotating in a cylindrical cavity with Dirichlet boundary conditions, interacting with a massless scalar field. They derive master equations and analyze resonant conditions for steady-state entanglement.
result: Steady-state entanglement is obtained under two resonant conditions, with higher concurrence achievable by tuning orbital radii. The system reduces to a dissipative Dicke model for identical atoms.
conclusion: The work provides an effective method for extracting steady-state entanglement from vacuum via the Unruh effect, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Green’s Function Methods For Computing Supercurrents In Josephson Junctions
authors: Eduardo R Mucciolo, Jouko Nieminen, Xiao Xiao, Wei-Chi Chiu, Michael N Leuenberger And Arun Bansil
abstract: Interest in Josephson junctions (JJs) has increased rapidly in recent years not only because of their use in qubits and other quantum devices but also due to the unique physics supported by the JJs. The advent of various novel quantum materials for both the barrier region and the superconducting leads has led to the possibility of adding new functionalities to the JJs. Thus, there is a growing need for accurate modeling of the JJs and related systems to enable their predictive control and atomistic level understanding. This review presents an in-depth discussion of a Green’s-function-based formalism for computing supercurrents in JJs. The formulation is tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations and encompasses both dc and ac supercurrents. We hope that this review will provide a timely and comprehensive reference for researchers as well as beginning practitioners interested in Green’s-function-based methods to model supercurrents in JJs.
tldr: A review of Green's function methods for computing supercurrents in Josephson junctions, focusing on large-scale atomistic simulations.
motivation: Josephson junctions are key components in qubits and quantum devices, and accurate modeling is needed for predictive control and atomistic understanding.
method: The paper presents a Green's-function-based formalism tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations to compute both dc and ac supercurrents.
result: The formalism enables accurate modeling of supercurrents in Josephson junctions with novel quantum materials.
conclusion: This review provides a comprehensive reference for researchers interested in Green's-function-based modeling of supercurrents in Josephson junctions.

title: Observation Of Alignment Tensor Effects In Metastability-exchange Collisions With Highly Polarized 3 ...
authors: Yida Sha, Kaiwen Yi, Xingqing Jin, Matteo Fadel And Xiang Peng
abstract: Highly polarized ensembles prepared by metastability-exchange optical pumping (MEOP) have been widely used in precision measurements and fundamental physics. Metastability-exchange (ME) collisions, serving as the basis of MEOP, are traditionally described in terms of atomic orientation, while the significant contributions of metastable alignment tensor at high polarization remain unexplored. In this work, we develop a linearized model under mean-field approximation to investigate alignment tensor effects in highly polarized , which originate from the metastable manifold and are revealed through ME-induced relaxation and frequency shift. By means of free-induction-decay measurements, a pronounced dependence on nuclear polarization is experimentally observed in the response of the ground-state-metastable hybrid ensembles to the external magnetic field. Furthermore, after obtaining the characteristics of tensor-induced phenomena, we demonstrate good agreement between the experiment and the theory. This work advances the understanding of nuclear spin dynamics in highly polarized using MEOP. It further provides applications in systematic error correction of high-accuracy magnetometry, as well as in optimal protocol for the generation of nuclear spin-squeezed states.
tldr: This paper studies alignment tensor effects in metastability-exchange collisions for highly polarized 3He, focusing on nuclear spin dynamics and magnetometry applications.
motivation: To understand alignment tensor contributions in metastability-exchange optical pumping at high polarization, which are not captured by traditional orientation-based models.
method: Develops a linearized mean-field model and validates it with free-induction-decay measurements on hybrid ground-state-metastable ensembles.
result: Observes a pronounced dependence of the ensemble response on nuclear polarization, and achieves good agreement between theory and experiment.
conclusion: Advances understanding of nuclear spin dynamics in highly polarized 3He and provides applications for systematic error correction in magnetometry and generation of spin-squeezed states.

title: Strain-driven Transition From Correlated Insulating To Semimetallic States In Twisted-bilayer Graphene
authors: Lishuai Guo, Abulimiti Yasen, Mei Xiang, Wenliang Zhu And Minghu Pan
abstract: We investigate the interplay between Coulomb interaction and uniaxial heterostrain in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) using a self-consistent Hartree–Fock (HF) approach projected onto the flat bands. For integer filling factors in the range of , we find that heterostrain strongly reconstructs the low-energy band structure and suppresses interaction-induced insulating gaps. As strain magnitude increases, the flat-band bandwidth is substantially enhanced, leading to an increased kinetic energy. The bandwidth enhancement effectively weakens the interaction strength relative to kinetic energy, resulting in the suppression of HF gaps and the emergence of semimetallic (SM) states. The strain effect can be primarily controlled by the filling factor, as well as the strain direction. At moderate strain strengths around 0.3% for , it can drive transitions between correlated insulating and SM states. In contrast, for , the HF gaps becomes negligible and the system remains essentially SM; both the strain direction and magnitude have negligible influence. Our results demonstrate that uniaxial heterostrain serves as an effective and versatile parameter for tuning correlated phases in TBG through the interplay of lattice deformation and Coulomb interactions.
tldr: This paper studies strain-driven transitions between correlated insulating and semimetallic states in twisted bilayer graphene using Hartree-Fock calculations.
motivation: Understanding how uniaxial heterostrain affects correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene, which is a key material in condensed matter physics.
method: Self-consistent Hartree-Fock approach projected onto flat bands to compute band structure and interaction-induced gaps under varying strain.
result: Heterostrain enhances bandwidth, suppresses insulating gaps, and drives transitions to semimetallic states; effect depends on filling factor and strain direction.
conclusion: Uniaxial heterostrain is an effective tuning parameter for correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene.

title: Observation Of Floquet Tensor Monopoles
authors: Hao Yuan, Weixuan Zhang, Na Sun And Xiangdong Zhang
abstract: Tensor monopoles, topological singularities of Kalb–Ramond tensor gauge fields, have garnered widespread attention in high-energy and condensed matter physics. They give rise to exotic phenomena such as quantized magnetoelectric responses and chiral boundary states, acting as potential building blocks for the development of topological devices in high-dimensional space. However, theoretical studies and experimental realizations reported to date have remained in static settings, and the realization of Floquet tensor monopoles (FTMs) and their associated anomalous non-equilibrium topological features has yet to be achieved. Here, we report the first theoretical and experimental implementation of FTMs in a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system. We systematically uncover the driving-frequency controlled creation, motion, and annihilation of FTMs, together with their anomalous bulk-edge correspondence. These phenomena are unique to FTMs and have no static counterparts. In experiments, we design and fabricate time-varying topological circuits, and directly observe the controllable motion of FTMs in k-space and their induced 3D Fermi-arc surface states by tuning the driving frequency. Our findings extend tensor monopole research to the non-equilibrium regime, providing a theoretical and experimental platform for exploring exotic topological phases in dynamic tensor gauge fields and laying the groundwork for functional topological devices with real-time control.
tldr: This paper reports the first experimental observation of Floquet tensor monopoles in a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system, demonstrating their creation, motion, and annihilation controlled by driving frequency.
motivation: Tensor monopoles have been studied in static settings, but their non-equilibrium counterparts (Floquet tensor monopoles) and associated anomalous topological features had not been realized.
method: The authors design and fabricate time-varying topological circuits to realize a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system, and observe the controllable motion of Floquet tensor monopoles in momentum space and their induced 3D Fermi-arc surface states by tuning the driving frequency.
result: They observe driving-frequency controlled creation, motion, and annihilation of Floquet tensor monopoles, along with anomalous bulk-edge correspondence unique to the non-equilibrium regime.
conclusion: This work extends tensor monopole research to non-equilibrium systems, providing a platform for exploring exotic topological phases in dynamic tensor gauge fields and functional topological devices with real-time control.

title: A Less-for-more Metamaterial Paradigm Via Laplace-Helmholtz Correspondence
authors: Zihang Guo, Fubao Yang, Tong Li, Shuihua Yang, Cheng-Wei Qiu, Jingjing He And Liujun Xu
abstract: The Laplace and Helmholtz equations dominate two fundamentally distinct physical processes: steady diffusion with a single constitutive parameter versus dynamic wave propagation with two. Manipulating complex wave dynamics through simple steady fields is typically deemed infeasible. Here, we bridge this gap by establishing the Laplace-Helmholtz correspondence, enabling a ‘less-for-more’ paradigm for metamaterial design. Rooted in a wave invariant, this framework allows the rigorous derivation of the two parameters and oscillatory field for the Helmholtz equation (the ‘more’) solely from the single parameter and steady field of the Laplace equation (the ‘less’). We demonstrate this capability by unlocking functionalities previously considered intractable, such as hyperbolic invisibility and three-dimensional freeform conformal cloaking with broadband performance. We further experimentally validate our strategy via a waveguide cloak. Our results bridge static and dynamic physics, establishing a versatile gateway for manipulating waves beyond conventional constraints.
tldr: This paper establishes a mathematical correspondence between Laplace and Helmholtz equations to design metamaterials for wave manipulation using static diffusion fields.
motivation: To bridge the gap between static and dynamic physics, enabling complex wave functionalities (e.g., hyperbolic invisibility, 3D cloaking) through simpler steady-state design.
method: The authors derive a wave invariant that maps the single-parameter Laplace equation to the two-parameter Helmholtz equation, allowing wave parameters and fields to be obtained from static solutions.
result: They demonstrate hyperbolic invisibility and 3D freeform conformal cloaking with broadband performance, and experimentally validate a waveguide cloak.
conclusion: The Laplace-Helmholtz correspondence provides a versatile gateway for manipulating waves beyond conventional constraints, enabling a 'less-for-more' paradigm in metamaterial design.

title: Pseudo-Hermitian Magnon Dynamics
authors: Xi-Guang Wang And Jamal Berakdar
abstract: A defining quantity of a physical system is its energy which is represented by the Hamiltonian. In closed quantum mechanical or/and fully coherent wave-based systems the Hamiltonian is introduced as a Hermitian operator which ensures real energy spectrum and secures the decomposition of any state over a complete basis set that spans the space where states live. Pseudo-Hermitian, or PT symmetric, systems are a special class of non-Hermitian ones. They describe open systems but may still have real energy spectrum. The eigenmodes are however not orthogonal in general. This qualitative difference to Hermitian physics has a range of consequences for the physical behavior of the system in the steady state or when it is subjected to external perturbations. This overview reviews the recent progress in the field of pseudo-Hermitian physics as it unfolds when applied to low-energy excitations of magnetically ordered materials. The focus is mainly on long wavelength spin excitations (spin waves) with magnons being the energy quanta of these excitations. Various setups including ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures with different types of coupling to the environments as well as spatio-temporally engineered systems will be discussed with a focus on the particular aspects that are brought about by the pseudo-Hermiticity such as mode amplification, non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, PT-symmetric assisted Floquet engineering, topological energy transfer, and field-induced enhanced sensitivity.
tldr: A review of pseudo-Hermitian magnon dynamics in magnetically ordered materials, focusing on non-Hermitian effects like mode amplification and non-reciprocal propagation.
motivation: To explore the unique physics of pseudo-Hermitian (PT-symmetric) systems in the context of magnon excitations, which offer new phenomena not present in Hermitian systems.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental progress on pseudo-Hermitian magnonics, covering various setups such as ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures.
result: Key phenomena include mode amplification, non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, PT-symmetric Floquet engineering, topological energy transfer, and enhanced sensitivity.
conclusion: Pseudo-Hermitian magnonics is a rapidly developing field with potential applications in spintronics and magnonics, but it is not directly aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Comprehensive Review On Master Stability Functions In Complex Network Dynamics
authors: Priodyuti Pradhan And Chandrakala Meena Suman Acharyya
abstract: Synchronization is a fundamental emergent phenomenon observed across a wide range of natural and engineered systems. Understanding the stability of a synchronization phenomenon is crucial for ensuring functionality in various complex systems. The master stability function (MSF) framework has emerged as a powerful and elegant tool for analyzing the stability of synchronization in coupled dynamical systems. By separating the effects of the node dynamics from the network structure, the MSF offers deep insights into synchronization behavior. However, a major challenge lies in determining the MSF for complex dynamical networks driven by nonlinear interaction mechanisms. These mechanisms introduce additional complexity due to the intricate connectivity of the interacting elements and the complex dynamics governed by nonlinear processes, diverse parameters, and the higher dimensionality of the system. Although MSF analysis has been widely used for more than past 25 years, a comprehensive and systematic investigation of MSF across various networked systems is still lacking. In this article, we present a simplified and unified analysis for the MSF in various undirected and directed networked systems. We begin by formulating the MSF framework in pairwise coupled identical systems and extend our analysis to directed networks and multilayer networks, considering both intralayer and interlayer interactions. Furthermore, we analyze the MSF formalism for higher-order networks. To facilitate understanding, we complement the theoretical developments with numerical analysis of synchronization stability in coupled systems. We also propose algorithms for computing the MSF, identifying stability regimes, and classifying the MSF behaviors. Overall, the primary goal of this review is to present a systematic study of the MSF in various coupled dynamical networks in a clear and structured manner, making this powerful tool more accessible. Furthermore, we highlight underexplored areas in the application of the MSF and discuss emerging directions, such as estimating the MSF using machine learning approaches.
tldr: A comprehensive review of the master stability function framework for analyzing synchronization stability in complex networks, covering pairwise, directed, multilayer, and higher-order networks.
motivation: Synchronization is a key emergent phenomenon in natural and engineered systems, and understanding its stability is crucial. Despite 25 years of MSF analysis, a systematic and unified treatment across various network types is lacking.
method: The paper formulates the MSF framework for pairwise coupled identical systems, then extends to directed networks, multilayer networks (intra- and interlayer), and higher-order networks. Numerical simulations and algorithms for computing MSF and classifying stability regimes are provided.
result: A simplified and unified MSF analysis is presented for undirected, directed, multilayer, and higher-order networks, with numerical examples demonstrating stability regimes.
conclusion: The review systematizes MSF analysis across diverse network topologies, making the tool more accessible, and highlights underexplored areas and future directions such as machine learning-based MSF estimation.

title: Classification And Correlation Signatures Of Chiral Spin Liquids On The Pyrochlore Lattice
authors: Leon Balents And Yasir Iqbal Chunxiao Liu
abstract: We present a systematic classification and variational study of chiral quantum spin liquids on the pyrochlore lattice based on fermionic parton constructions. Focusing on chiral and spin-liquid Ansätze, we characterize their symmetry properties, flux structures, and low-energy spinon spectra within a projective symmetry group framework, and incorporate gauge fluctuations through Gutzwiller-projected wave functions studied by variational Monte Carlo. From the equal-time spin structure factor, we develop correlation-based diagnostics that distinguish gauge-dominated Coulomb phases from states with substantial matter-field and short-range contributions. Distinct chiral flux sectors, though close in energy, exhibit markedly different degrees of emergent gauge-field dominance, reflected in the geometry and contrast of pinch-point singularities. Although these states are not competitive ground states of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model, they define a physically meaningful family of proximate chiral phases relevant to extended pyrochlore Hamiltonians.
tldr: This paper classifies chiral spin liquids on the pyrochlore lattice using parton constructions and variational Monte Carlo, focusing on symmetry and correlation signatures.
motivation: Chiral spin liquids are exotic quantum phases with potential relevance to frustrated magnets, but their classification on the pyrochlore lattice is incomplete.
method: The authors use fermionic parton theory with projective symmetry groups to classify chiral Ansätze, and study Gutzwiller-projected wave functions via variational Monte Carlo to compute spin structure factors.
result: Distinct chiral flux sectors are identified, showing varying degrees of gauge-field dominance reflected in pinch-point singularities, though they are not ground states of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model.
conclusion: The work provides a family of proximate chiral phases for extended pyrochlore Hamiltonians, but does not directly advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Physical Sampling For Computational Photography
authors: Ni Chen And David J Brady
abstract: The standard model of photography is that lenses form images and focal planes capture those images. Over the past two decades, however, cameras have been transformed from devices that record focal images into analog-to-digital converters that transform massively parallel optical signals into serial electronic data. Under this new model, one may choose to maximize the quality and quantity of captured information, rather than focal image quality. Here we review the nature of the optical data stream and consider lens and focal plane designs that improve information capture capacity. After maximizing information capacity, the challenge of converting this information to digital data requires novel read-out and compression. We review strategies for approaching physical information limits under realistic size, power, and bandwidth constraints. Multiscale monocentric (spherical primary optics combined with arrays of secondary micro-cameras, each imaging a narrow subfield) and array lens architectures relax unfavorable geometric scaling by trading monolithic optics for co-designed system-level integration (jointly optimized optics, focal-plane, and readout subsystems). Metaoptic and mode-sorting focal plane filters implement richer projection operators that sample spectral, polarimetric, and coherence features without requiring exhaustive scanning. Finally, because readout and computation dominate energy at high throughput, we highlight architectures that perform dimensionality reduction before (or during) digitization, including integrated photonic encoders and multilayer optical projections coupled to detection and learned decoding.
